Participants provided answers to general information questions, rated their confidence, and then decided whether to stick with their answer or be given the correct answer by the computer.
In all experiments, participants were told to maximize the number of points earned, allowing us to investigate whether people optimize offloading decisions.

Further, participants were relatively insensitive to the value of the options, even in a condition in which the rational choice to maximize points was to offload everything and ignore metacognition entirely.

Participants gave their answers and their confidence judgments about whether they believed their answers to be correct, and then had to decide whether they wanted to stick with their answers or receive the correct answer from the computer (offload).
Participants were given different number of points, across experiments, for choosing to stick or to offload.

Participants were asked to give their answers to a series of general information questions, to give their confidence judgments about whether they believed their answers to be correct, and then to decide whether they wanted to stick with their answers or to offload to the computer.
Forty participants were recruited via Prolific.co.
In Experiment 1 we recruited 40 participants.

Four participants timed out before finishing the study, leaving a total of 36 adults (23 female, 13 male), ranging in age from 18 to 30 years (x̄ = 24.8, SD = 3.4) with x̄ = 14.8 (SD = 2.5) years of education in the current analysis.
Participants had up to 15 seconds to answer each question.

After giving their confidence ratings and offloading decisions to all questions, they were shown the correct answers to all questions in a random order for 3 seconds each, and then they were given a final recall test in which questions were presented in a random order and participants had up to 15 seconds to respond to each.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .05", Text = "In Experiment 1, this correlation was significantly positive (r = 0.57, t(34) = 4.02, p < .05), as is shown in the left panel of Figure 4."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. info.title: The Metacognitive Underpinnings of Offloading Decisions

text.text: In five experiments, we investigated how people's metacognitive assessments influence their decisions about whether to rely on their own answers to questions or to obtain the answers from an external source (i.e., to offload).
Participants provided answers to general information questions, rated their confidence, and then decided whether to stick with their answer or be given the correct answer by the computer.

To examine how metacognitive accuracy impacts offloading, experiment 2-5 included condition which produced good resolution (using easy and difficult questions), and condition that produced poor resolution (using questions people typically think they know the answers to, but don't).
The value of offloading was also varied across experiments via the assignment of differing numbers of "points" for sticking or offloading.
In all experiments, participants were told to maximize the number of points earned, allowing us to investigate whether people optimize offloading decisions.
Across all five experiments, participants' confidence in their answers predicted whether they would offload or not: when confidence was high, they did not offload; when it was low, they offloaded.
They did this even when their metacognition was faulty.

Further, participants were relatively insensitive to the value of the options, even in a condition in which the rational choice to maximize points was to offload everything and ignore metacognition entirely.

These findings indicate that, even when metacognitive evaluations are either wrong or irrelevant (rather than being correct and germane), people's offloading choices are strongly influenced by their metacognition.
Cognitive offloading is the process of delegating to outside resources, tools, or people, assistance in accomplishing a cognitive task.
This article investigates the role of metacognition in people's decisions to offload.
Offloading in some situations can be beneficial.
People may sometimes use it to overcome their own shortcomings and still achieve a valuable outcome.

Its use is sometimes assumed to imply that people have an intention to either reduce their own mental load and save mental energy for more important tasks (Grinschgl & Neubauer, 2022; Risko & Gilbert, 2016), while still achieving the desired goal.

text.text: But, of course, offloading may not always be beneficial.

Indeed, it may sometimes be counterproductive, and undermine human development, cognitive capabilities and wellbeing (Gerlich, 2025; Grinschgl, Papenmeier, & Meyerhoff, 2021; Henkel, 2014; Kelly & Risko, 2019; Marsh & Rajaram, 2019; Sparrow, Lui, & Wegner, 2011).

text.text: This concern is particularly salient now that answers to questions small and large are readily, easily, and endlessly available through AI (Bastani et al, 2025; Rismanchian et al, 2026; Yu et al., 2026).

text.text: To have the knowledge needed to promote the proactive, beneficial use of cognitive offloading, an understanding of the factors that affect whether and when people choose to offload to an external source or instead rely on their own knowledge is necessary.
Much prior work has examined prospective memory offloading, in which a future cognitive demand is outsourced.
For example, people might set an external reminder to wish a friend happy birthday, or make a grocery list rather than trying to remember what they need to get once they are in the store.

In these contexts, offloading may be beneficial and allow people to externalize future, potentially faulty, cognitive processes that would otherwise have to be performed internally, and thus it may increase the chance of a favorable outcome (Berry, Allen, Mon-Williams, & Waterman, 2019; Burnett & Richmond, 2026; Gilbert, 2024; Hertzog & Dunlosky, 2011; Martin et al, 2022; Shetye, 2024; Storm & Stone, 2015).

text.text: But offloading need not always be prospective, and it does not require that no internal processing has occurred already: a decision to offload can occur even after a person has tried to do the task themselves.
In the TV trivia show 'Who Wants to be a Millionaire?', for example, contestants are tasked with coming up with the correct answer to difficult questions.
They often try hard to generate an answer on their own, but they may vary in their uncertainty about the result.
To achieve their goal, they may decide to stick with their own answer, or they may use one of their 'lifelines,' thereby offloading--asking an external source for the answer.
People's knowledge about their own knowledge --their metacognitive evaluations on an item-by-item level--is likely to be key for understanding what they decide to do.

To offload effectively, we propose that people, in most cases, need to be able to accurately identify when their own knowledge (and capabilities, in the prospective case) is sufficient to answer correctly (and see, Boldt & Gilbert, 2019; Gilbert, Bird, Carpenter, Fleming, Sachdeva, & Tsai, 2020; Grinschgl, Meyerhoff, Schwan, & Papenmeier,2021; Hu, Luo, & Fleming, 2019; Ngia & Gilbert, 2026).

text.text: If they are highly confident that they have sufficient knowledge, they should anticipate no need to offload; if they are not as confident, the felt need should increase.
The accuracy of those metacognitive assessments should, of course, alter how effective such as strategy is.

But effective offloading may depend not only on the goodness of metacognition, but also on the costs and benefits of taking the cognitive task upon oneself as compared to taking on external assistance.
If there are a limited number of offloading opportunities, or if opportunities are more rather than less costly, offloading decisions should be reserved for when they are most needed.

If, on the other hand, there is no cost to offloading or when offloading is more valuable than sticking with doing a task oneself, offloading may be a rational choice, regardless of how confident the person is in their own knowledge and abilities.
Across five experiments, we explored the relation between metacognition and offloading by asking participants to answer a series of general information questions.

Participants gave their answers and their confidence judgments about whether they believed their answers to be correct, and then had to decide whether they wanted to stick with their answers or receive the correct answer from the computer (offload).
Participants were given different number of points, across experiments, for choosing to stick or to offload.
We then provided correct feedback and retested participants on all questions.

Across the five experiments, we used general information questions that showed a wide range of metacognitive judgments to examine the hypothesis that people's offloading decisions closely follow their individual item-specific metacognitive ratings in a systematic manner.
The first experiment investigated the simple relation between metacognition and offloading, at the item-by-item level, and did not vary the materials to manipulate people's metacognitive accuracy.

The question was straightforward: Do people choose to substitute the computer's answer for their own answers to general knowledge questions that they think they might not know the answers to, and stick with their own answers when they believe that they know?
In Experiment 2 and the subsequent experiments, metacognitive accuracy was manipulated.
In these four experiments, we used two types of questions.
In the 'good metacognition' condition, the materials afforded excellent metacognition.
Questions were either very easy or very difficult, and people's metacognitive judgments were objectively close to perfect: they knew which answers they knew and which they did not know.
In the 'poor metacognition' condition, the materials used resulted in inaccurate judgments: People often thought they knew the answers when, in reality, they did not.

While we still expected that their individual offloading decisions would follow their metacognitive judgments, we also expected that in the condition in which those judgments were highly accurate, their offloading would be close to 'optimal', that is, participants would make decisions about whether or not to offload that would come close to maximizing attainable points (see Murphy & Metcalfe, 2025).

text.text: In contrast, in the condition in which those judgments were inaccurate, we predicted that their offloading optimality would suffer.
In Experiments 1 and 2, participants received 10 points for sticking if they were correct, and 0 points if they were wrong.
In both experiments, they received 5 points if they chose to offload, regardless of whether the answer they had given was right or wrong.

In Experiment 3 and 4, we increased and decreased value of the points earned for offloading or sticking to explore whether the cost of offloading influenced how people used their metacognitive judgments.
In other words, did they adjust their metacognitive criterion for offloading as a function of how many points they would get for offloading?
And did alterations in the magnitude of point values influence offloading optimality?
In both experiments, they received 10 points if they stuck with their answer and were correct.
Experiment 3 participants received 8 points for offloading, whereas in Experiment 4 they received only 2 points for offloading.
Finally, in the fifth experiment, the assignment of offloading points was taken to a logical extreme: this time, if they offloaded, they got 10 points.

Thus, rationally, to maximize points, participants should have disregarded their metacognition entirely: even if they were 99.99999% sure they were right, they should always chose the sure payout of 10 points, just in case they were wrong.

Overview of experiments' question types and payoff structures.
In Experiment 1, we sought to examine the relation between metacognitive judgments and offloading decisions in a straightforward manner.

Participants were asked to give their answers to a series of general information questions, to give their confidence judgments about whether they believed their answers to be correct, and then to decide whether they wanted to stick with their answers or to offload to the computer.
If they stuck they would get 10 points if correct, but zero points if wrong.
If they offloaded, they would get 5 points for that question whether they were right or wrong.

We hypothesized that when people were above some confidence criterion related to the relative payoff for sticking and offloading, they would stick with their answer, whereas when they were below that criterion, they would offload.

We expected that the particular payoff structure in this first experiment would probably result in people choosing to stick with their answer if their confidence was above 50%, and offload if their confidence was below 50%.

text.text: Participants in this experiment were presented with 50 general information questions, each of which had a unique correct answer that was a noun, one at a time in a random order.
Participants had up to 15 seconds to answer each question.
They then provided a confidence rating indicating their feeling that their answer was correct on a scale from 0 ("sure wrong") to 100 ("sure right").
Finally, they choose whether they wanted to stick with their own answer or offload to the computer for the answer.
They were told, before the task began, both about the point structure, and that their job was to maximize the number of points they obtained.

After giving their confidence ratings and offloading decisions to all questions, they were shown the correct answers to all questions in a random order for 3 seconds each, and then they were given a final recall test in which questions were presented in a random order and participants had up to 15 seconds to respond to each.
The questions derived from Funnell, Metcalfe, and Tsapkini (1996), and all answers to these questions were uniquely specified nouns.

text.text: For instance, two questions were: "The largest bird on earth that cannot fly is the _______." and "The type of snake that Asia snake charmers' charm is the ____________."
We used this set of questions because it has several properties that make it well-suited to studying metacognition and offloading.
First, the control participants in the Funnell et al. experiment got about half (i.e., 43%) correct.

Thus, the set is neither so easy that everyone already knows the answers (which would leave no room for offloading to matter) nor so hard that no one had any relevant knowledge to draw on (which would leave no room for metacognitive judgments to be informative).

Second, the distributions of metacognitive judgments on this set were fairly evenly distributed across the range of ratings (see Figure 3 in Funnell et al., 1996), indicating that people genuinely use the whole range of confidence when judging these items.

text.text: The MOOT scores that give the corresponding optimality of people's offloading decisions are directly below in that figure.
With high resolution, such as is shown here, the expectation was that MOOT scores would also be high.

To assess the optimality of offloading, it is insufficient to simply count the number of points attained, since the objective correctness of responding impacts this score: participants with more correct responses have more opportunities to do well and have higher scores than do those with fewer correct responses, since those correct scores are necessary for obtaining 10s--the value given to correct-stick responses.
It is therefore necessary to take the person's baseline performance into account.

We did so by computing each participant's "MOOT" score (proposed and so named by Murphy & Metcalfe, 2025, from their 'Metacognitive Offloading Optimality Task,' which, like the present task, allows discernment of how many items individual participants got correct).

text.text: We next investigated the across-participant Pearson correlation between gamma scores (which indicate the individual's overall metacognitive sensitivity) and MOOT scores (which indicate the optimality of their offloading).

A positive correlation would indicate that people who have better metacognition (they better discriminate their correct from incorrect responses) also offload more optimally, whereas those with less good metacognition offload less optimally.
Such a positive correlation would suggest that offloading to effectively gain the points depends on accurate selfknowledge.

A correlation near zero would suggest offloading optimality is largely independent of metacognitive sensitivity, driven instead by something else, such as a fixed strategy, a disregard of the point structure, or consideration of some other socio-emotional or cognitive factor such as general caution.
A negative correlation would imply that greater metacognitive sensitivity is associated with worse offloading.

text.text: In the second experiment, we investigated the consequences of good and poor metacognition on offloading behavior, which we manipulated using two sets of intermixed materials.
The first set included both Easy and Difficult questions.
Data from past research using these questions showed that people have very good metacognitive resolution for these questions.
An example of an easy question is: What do you call a female deer?
Nearly everyone gets the correct answer, and nearly everyone is highly confident that they got it right.
An example of a difficult question is: What is the last name of the current ruling dynasty of Monaco?
Most people get this wrong --usually by omission--but they also know that they are wrong.
Thus, metacognitive resolution on the set of Easy/Difficult items is high.
The other set of questions included items which frequently evoke an illusion of knowing.
The questions in this set are items on which people often think they know the answer --and express high confidence in their answers--but don't.
We call this set of items the "ThoughtYouKnew" condition.
The kind of materials in the ThoughtYouKnew condition are of considerable interest and have been studied by many theorists.
An example is "What country was the new Volkswagen Beetle produced in?"
Most people get this wrong, but yet think, often with high confidence, that they know the answer.
There is an answer comes to mind easily and fluently but yet is wrong.
These types of questions are frequently associated with high intersubject consensuality on a particular incorrect answer.

North American participants often are highly confident that the new Volkswagen Beetle was produced in Germany, that the capital of Australia is Sydney, that the longest river in the United States is the Mississippi, that the eastern-most state is Maine, and that bats navigate over long distances by echolocation.
Similar materials, on which people are consensually wrong, have been extensively studied by Koriat.
Although he sometimes used line drawings and figures with these characteristics (Koriat, 2011), we here used general information questions.

text.text: We here, chose to refer to these items as ThoughtYouKnew, to avoid any insinuation that these items contain any nefarious intent to make people believe something that is false (which would likewise be the case if we referred to them as 'Misconceptions').

Instead, we call them ThoughtYouKnew, simply because people tend, fairly consistently, to get the answers wrong while thinking that they are right, which is, by definition, poor metacognition--they don't know that they don't know.

The fact that these tend to be items on which people frequently make high confidence errors is also of interest because (a) people are especially curious about such items (Metcalfe, Vuorre, Towner, & Eich, 2023) (b) people often agree in their spurious judgments that the wrong answers are correct, that is, there is consensus concerning these items (Brewer & Sampaio, 2012) (c) they strongly contribute to pervasive and deleterious overconfidence effects, (d) once they are told the correct answer, both adults and children often say that they knew it all along (Finn & Metcalfe, 2007 , 2008 , Metcalfe & Finn, 2011), (e) they often have considerable amount of information surrounding such items; that is such items come from dense semantic landscapes (Sitzman, Rhodes, Tauber, & Liceralde, 2015; Eich et al, 2026), and (f) rather than doubling down on the wrong answer, once people are provided with the correct answer, they have a tendency to hypercorrect these items, that is to remember the correct answer when it is provided (Butterfield & Metcalfe, 2006, though note there is some regression toward the original, erroneous response over time, Butler, Fazio, & Marsh, 2011).

text.text: Despite their interest, such high confidence errors (or items that people 'thought they knew' but didn't) tend to be relatively rare.
Accordingly, we built a larger-than-usual pool of such items for use here (see Appendix A).

To investigate the relation between metacognition and offloading, we here contrasted people's offloading behavior on the set of items on which their metacognition was good (the Easy/Difficult condition) with their offloading behavior on the set on which their metacognition was poor (the ThoughtYouKnew condition).

Our hypothesis was straightforward: When the influence of other factors--factors that we acknowledge could often play an important role in real-world offloading such as feelings of curiosity or boredom, stress, severe time constraints, and so on--was minimized, offloading should be more optimal when metacognition was good than poor.

We tried to eliminate other factors by using a game framing, as in Experiment 1, where participants tried to get as many points as possible by either sticking with their own answer or offloading to the computer to get the answer right and attain points.
And we used the same point allocation as in Experiment 1.
We expected, then, that people would produce higher gamma scores indicating better metacognitive resolution in the Easy/Difficult condition than in the ThoughtYouKnew condition.
If offloading was related to metacognition, we hypothesized that offloading optimality would also be higher in the Easy/Difficult condition than in the ThoughtYouKnew condition.

When metacognition was excellent, as was the case in the Easy/Difficult condition, people offloaded close to optimally; when it was mediocre, as was the case in the ThoughtYouKnew condition, the optimality of their offloading suffered.
This relation provides clear evidence for the strong connection between metacognition and offloading.

If offloading is titrated to the payoff structure of the situation, it should be based not only on people's metacognition, but also on the relative point value assigned to sticking as compared to offloading.
In the first two experiments, the confidence scale was divided at the midpoint, and sticking was worth 10 points if correct and 0 points if wrong, whereas offloading was worth 5 points regardless.
In both experiments, the inflection point was also at the midpoint.

That is, because the points awarded for offloading were set at exactly half the points awarded for a correct stick response, the confidence level at which the expected value of sticking equals the guaranteed value of offloading is 50% -the midpoint of the confidence scale.
Thus, a participant should stick whenever their confidence exceeds 50% (since expected value of sticking then exceeds the guaranteed offload payoff) and offload whenever it falls below 50%.
But, if the values changed, so too should the inflection point.
If offloaded items were worth almost as much as items on which people gave the answers themselves, they might be inclined to offload more.
Conversely, if offloaded items were worth very little, they might be inclined to offload only infrequently.
There is some experimental support for the hypothesis that people's offloading behavior is sensitive to the value of the offloaded items.
For instance, Murphy (2023) created a prospective memory situation in which items could be offloaded to an external memory store rather than remembered at a later time.
When he indicated to participants that the external store might be unreliable or limited, people offloaded to it less frequently than they did when they were told it was reliable and unlimited.
It was as if they had devalued the offloading option, and altered their behavior accordingly.

Similarly, when Murphy and Metcalfe (2025), again in a prospective memory paradigm, varied the point values given for later remembering items oneself as compared to offloading them to be remembered by the computer, people's choices to offload were affected.

text.text: When points assigned for offloaded items were high, people offloaded more than when the points given for offloaded items were low.

This prospective memory task was different from the present task, since the metacognitive judgments as well as the goal of the task, were directed at the probability of future (not present) correct responding.

Additionally, people may have taken into account the effort that might be needed (and perhaps how valuable that cognitive effort itself was in relation to the point payoff) to make that later correct responding possible.

Nevertheless, these studies suggested that people were likely to be sensitive to the value of the offloaded items, and might alter their metacognitive threshold for offloading depending upon that value.

To investigate the hypothesis that, in this paradigm, too, people would be sensitive to the value of the offloaded items, Experiments 3 and 4 investigated the effect of changing those values in opposite ways.
Experiment 3 made offloading more valuable (worth 8 points), while Experiment 4 made it less valuable (worth 2 points) than the midpoint value (5 points) investigated in Experiments 1 and 2.

If people were sensitive to the value of sticking versus offloading, then this change in point value assigned to 'offloaded' as compared to 'stick' items should produce a shift in the inflection point of the metacognitive function relating confidence to offloading.
They should offload at a lower confidence level when offloaded items were worth more and offload less --at a higher confidence threshold--when they were worth less.

The third experiment, then, was like the second, except that the point values in the third experiment gave a much greater weight to offloading, whilst still prioritizing sticking if one's certainty that one was right was very high.
In this experiment, instead of allocating 5 points for offloading, 8 points were allocated.
We expected that people would offload more in this experiment than in the previous one, and that the confidence inflection point at which they chose to offload would be lower.
The materials and procedure were identical to those used in the previous experiment.
The only difference was that participants were instructed that offloaded items were worth 8 points, rather than 5, points.

In both experiment 3 and 4, just as in Experiment 2, people were highly sensitive to their metacognitions.
They apparently used their confidence ratings to determine whether or not to offload.

Furthermore, when their metacognition was highly accurate, the optimality of their offloading decisions was high whereas when their metacognitive accuracy was low--in the ThoughtYouKnew condition--their offloading optimality was low.
It can be concluded from these findings that people were using their metacognition as the basis for their offloading decisions.
But, surprisingly, they appeared not to take the value of the offloaded items into account.

As is shown in Figure 5, there was no shift in the offloading threshold--the inflection point in people's metacognitive that marked the point at which they shifted from sticking to offloading-between any of the three experiments.

text.text: They shifted at around a confidence rating of .5 whether offloading was valued at 2 points per offloaded item, 5 points per offloaded item, or 8 points per offloaded item.
This failure to respond to the differential value of the offloaded items was a surprise to us.
Accordingly, we conducted some additional analyses to investigate why this might have happened.

One possibility for why people may not have altered the metacognitive threshold for offloading in these three experiments, is that the metacognitive judgments themselves may have been extremely bimodal.

People may not have based their judgments on intermediate analogue values of their confidence that took nuances about their degree of confidence that they were right into account, if those intermediate values were unavailable.
Perhaps they had only made a crude assessment of whether they thought they were right or not.
Such a binary assessment is still metacognition, but it would not reflect the nuances of a graded judgment that could support a change in the inflection point along a confidence continuum.
It was possible, for example, that people only used two points on our continuous confidence measure--100% sure they were right and 0% sure they were wrong.

If the confidence data were extremely bimodal, people might have changed their offload/stick criterion based on value, but it would not have mattered--we would not be able to discern it in the results.

To illustrate with an example, suppose all of people's responses were either those of which the were very sure of and gave a high confidence rating to of, let's say, over 80% or they were responses that they knew were wrong, to which they gave a confidence rating of less than 20%.
For sake of argument, suppose that half of their responses were .8 or above and the other half were 20% and below, and there were no rating between 20% and 80% confidence.
And, suppose they used a general strategy of sticking with high confidence items, and offloading low confidence items (as we know from the data they did, see Figure 1).

text.text: In Experiment 2 we would expect them to set the offloading criterion at 50% confidence, in Experiment 3 at 20% confidence and in Experiment 4 at 80% confidence.
Would the expected changes in the criterion make any difference in the observable data?
The answer is no.

In all three experiments, even with those very different offloading criteria, they would end up offloading all of the low confidence items and sticking with all of the high confidence items (and it would look like the inflection point was 50% in all three cases even though people might have actually changed their criterion according to the difference in value in the three experiments).

There would be no difference in the observable criterion since there would be no items which had confidence ratings between 20% and 80% which would allow us to differentiate between the three different hypothetical criterion settings.

We had designed the 'good metacognition' (Easy/Difficult) condition to allow people to know when they were right and when they were wrong: they should have shown very high confidence on the easy items and very low confidence on the difficult items (as, indeed, they did as shown in Figure 2).

text.text: And there should have been few items of intermediate confidence.

By the nature of the materials in the design for the Easy/Difficult conditions, then, we would expect such bi-model confidence distributions that would fail to afford observation of a criterion shift.
The faulty metacognition condition was different.

While acknowledging that it was possible, in principle, that extreme bimodality could have occurred in the ThoughtYouKnew condition, it was nevertheless the case that we had endeavored to include items that would elicit intermediate confidence judgments.
We had tried to include items that were high confidence errors usually or that were so-called 'deceptive' items.

We expected that people would probably have partial information in that condition (e.g., they would name a Canadian city as the capital of Canada, not an American city), and that such partial information would lend itself to more intermediate confidence ratings.

If so, then, although the Easy/Difficult condition perhaps could not, the ThoughtYouKnew condition could, potentially at least, allow observation of a metacognitively based criterion shift in offloading attributable to the different value of the offloaded items in Experiment 2, 3, and 4.

The fifth experiment looked at whether there was any value manipulation that would induce participants to take value into account.

This final experiment took the value manipulation to its logical extreme--an extreme at which participants could and should have optimized their scores by simply ignoring their metacognition entirely and offloading everything.
There would be no uncertainty in doing so, and they would get a perfect score if they did this.

As before, participants were told that they were supposed to maximize their point scores and that they would get 10 points for every item on which they decided to stick, but only if they were right--if they were wrong, they would get zero.
But in this final experiment, we told them that they would get 10 points for every item that they offloaded, regardless of whether they were right or wrong.
To make sure they processed these point values, we also implemented a comprehension check.

The method, materials, and procedure were identical to those used in Experiments 2, 3, and 4, except that participants were instructed that offloaded items were worth 10, and items on which they decided to stick were worth 10 if they were correct but 0 if they were incorrect.

text.text: Notably, there were 4 (but only 4) participants in this experiment who, rationally, offloaded everything.
A sensitivity analysis without these 4 participants did not change the overall results.
This set of experiments establishes that people's metacognition about whether they think they know or do not know the answers is a crucial factor in determining their offloading behavior.
If they think they know the answer to the question, they stick with their own answer.
If they think that they don't know the answer, they offload.
This item-level effect was replicated across all five experiments.

But, even though people stick with their answer when they are confident that they know and offload when they judge that they don't know, those metacognitive judgments are not, themselves, always accurate.
Experiments 2 through 5 investigated offloading optimality under conditions associated with good versus poor metacognitive resolution.

These experiments included a set of items on which people had good metacognitive resolution--they knew what they knew and didn't know--and a set on which they had poor metacognitive resolution--they thought they knew many of the answers that, objectively, they did not know.
In these experiments, when people's metacognitive resolution was excellent, their offloading was close to optimal.
When their metacognitive resolution was poor, on the other hand, their offloading suffered.
Here, optimality refers specifically and only to stated payoff optimality, that is, whether decisions about offloading maximized the attainable payoff within the task.
Its use, here, does not imply anything about the effects of offloading on people's longer-term cognitive abilities, their learning, subsequent independent performance, or enhanced human welfare.
Experiments 2, 3, and 4 also investigated whether people were sensitive to the value of the offloaded items.

Past research on value-directed remembering and cognitive offloading has demonstrated that individuals are often sensitive to payoff structures and can adjust their reliance on external memory stores to maximize objective rewards (e.g., Knowlton & Castel, 2022; Murphy, 2023; Murphy & Castel, 2023; Park, Kelly, Hargis, & Risko, 2022).

text.text: The present results, though, showed little sensitivity to the value assigned to offloaded items.
We had hypothesized that if we made offloaded items more valuable, people would have been more inclined to offload them and maximize their score.
Conversely, if offloaded items were worth less, people should have shifted their criterion to be willing to stick with items about which they had less confidence.
Experiments 3, and 4, however, failed to show this pattern of a shift in the confidence criterion for offloading as a function of the assigned value of the offloaded items.
One possibility for why there was no observable change in offloading criterion was that the metacognition itself might have been strongly bimodal.
If there were no intermediate assessments of partial knowing available to allow titration of the exact intermediate degree of confidence, people might be unable to be responsive to changes in value.
This was the case in the Easy/difficult condition in Experiments 2-4, but it was not the case in the ThoughtYouKnew condition.

However, both conditions equally failed to show the expected change in inflection point with changes in value that would have indicted that subtle metacognitively-dependent choice criterion changes that reflected the changes in values.

It is possible that in the condition in which people made a large number of intermediate confidence judgments (that potentially could have shown an effect of shifts in the value of offloading) that people used only a crude summary judgment of know/don't know in order to make their offloading decisions.
The failure to show a sensitivity to the value manipulation might have occurred at the decision level not the metacognitive level.

The lack of betweencondition differences in the inflection points, in combination with a notable difference in the amount of information at intermediate levels of confidence in the two conditions, suggests that although people had intermediate metacognitive information available that could have been used in response to changes in value, selectively, in the ThoughtYouKnew condition, they did not use that intermediate information in their offloading decisions.
The metacognition was subtle but the decisions were crude.
Importantly, though, in Experiment 5, when we increased the value of offloading items to an extreme extent, we were able to induce a shift in the offloading criterion.
That criterion went from approximately 50% confidence in Experiments 2-4 to 70% in Experiment 5.
Interestingly, though, even that shift was not enough to be considered fully rational.
In order to optimize reward, people, in Experiment 5, should have completely disregarded their metacognitive judgements, and offloaded 100% of the time.

Since people were sure of getting 10 points if they offloaded, and yet there was uncertainty about getting 10 points if they stuck with any of their own answers, people should have always taken the sure path.
But only 4 participants did this.
The remainder of the participants continued, irrationally, to use a metacognitive strategy that was almost indistinguishable from the one that was used in the four other experiments in this series.
They still stuck with their answers when they thought they knew and offloaded when they thought they did not know.

We speculate that, although this could certainly be viewed as irrational behavior, a less disparaging possibility is that sticking with one's own answers when one thinks one is correct (and offloading only selectively) has some intrinsic value in the real world even in the face of potentially decreased rewards in the context of our experiment.
Perhaps this strategy enhances learning, or perhaps it taps a deeply adaptive need for agency.
It may be highly beneficial in other contexts, where there is nearly always a tradeoff and one rarely gets things for free.
Further research is clearly needed to investigate why and when people engage in what seems, in this case, to objectively be a dysfunctional use of metacognition.

In conclusion, these results indicate that people do base their offloading decisions on their metacognition, and do so in a simple way: When they think they are right, they stick; when they think they are wrong, they offload.
When these metacognitive judgments are accurate, this strategy can lead to results that are close to optimal.

When the metacognitive judgments are wrong, however, as they frequently were in the ThoughtYouKnew condition of these experiments, this reliance on their metacognition results in suboptimal offloading.

Furthermore, the data presented here suggest--though more follow-up research is needed--that the strategy of depending upon a simple binary metacognitive signal may produce an insensitivity to the value of the items.
People used this same strategy, even when, as in Experiment 5, it was counterproductive to use a metacognitive strategy at all--they should have just offloaded everything to obtain maximum rewards.
But even when using this same metacognitive strategy was disadvantageous, people, nevertheless, persisted in it use.
